body: {"total":6,"records":[{"title":"Structured templates for abdominal CT reports and completeness of key findings: a multicentre before-after study","authors":"Achebe-Lindqvist O, Moreno-Hart P, Takeda-Brennan S","year":2023,"venue":"Journal of Radiology Reporting","doi":"10.5555/jrr.2023.0152","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Six hospitals introduced structured templates for abdominal CT and we compared 2,400 reports from six months before with 2,400 from six months after. The proportion of reports containing all pre-specified key elements for the clinical question rose from 64 to 91 percent. Median time from scan completion to report sign-off increased by 2 minutes. Six months after introduction, 88 percent of eligible reports used the template. Improvements were largest for suspected appendicitis and smallest for oncology staging, where free-text additions remained common."},{"title":"Radiologist adoption of structured reporting: template use over the first year in one department","authors":"Hollis-Adeyemi R, Sandberg-Oyelaran T","year":2020,"venue":"Radiology Practice Management","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We tracked template use for body CT in one department for twelve months after introduction. The template was opened for 94 percent of reports and fully completed for 71 percent; in 23 percent a radiologist overrode the template with free text for at least one section. Use plateaued after four months. Senior radiologists overrode the template more often than junior staff. Radiologists said overrides were most useful for complex or incidental findings. The authors recommend defining use as completion without override when evaluating adoption."},{"title":"Structured versus free-text radiology reports: a systematic review of report quality and referrer satisfaction","authors":"Ibanez-Kowalczyk M, Obi-Sorensen L, Grant-Nakamura A","year":2021,"venue":"Evidence Reviews in Imaging","doi":"10.5555/eri.2021.0063","providerType":"review","abstract":"We included 32 studies comparing structured with free-text radiology reports. Structured reports were more complete in 27 studies and referrer satisfaction was higher in 9 of the 11 studies that measured it. No study measured patient outcomes. Most studies were before-after comparisons in single departments, and completeness checklists were often designed with the template, which may favour structured reports. We found no evidence that structured reporting increased reporting errors. Few studies reported how often radiologists overrode templates, so adoption could rarely be judged alongside completeness."},{"title":"What referring clinicians want from CT reports for suspected appendicitis: a preference study","authors":"Varga-Oduya L, Castellanos-Fry D","year":2018,"venue":"Emergency Imaging Research","doi":"10.5555/eir.2018.0029","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We asked 146 surgeons and emergency physicians to choose between pairs of CT reports for suspected appendicitis that differed in structure, length and content. Clinicians valued an explicit statement of the appendix diameter, the presence or absence of free fluid and gas, and a clear one-line impression. Long reports reduced perceived usefulness even when complete. Emergency physicians valued the impression line more than surgeons did, while surgeons valued explicit measurements more. Responses came from three hospitals with established free-text reporting, so preferences may shift once clinicians are used to structured reports."},{"title":"Measuring completeness of historic free-text reports against a new structured checklist: rater agreement","authors":"Kristensen-Mbeki H, Duval-Achterberg N","year":2022,"venue":"Radiology Practice Management","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Two radiologists rated 300 free-text abdominal CT reports against a 12-item checklist written for a new structured template. Agreement was good (kappa 0.72). Completeness was underestimated when elements were implied rather than stated, for example when a normal appendix was described without a diameter. Applying a rule that counted an element as present when it was stated or clearly implied raised measured completeness of free-text reports by 9 percentage points. The authors recommend pre-specifying such a rule before any before-after comparison."},{"title":"Reporting time with structured templates in body CT: a time-stamp analysis","authors":"Petrov-Adair J, Nwachukwu-Holm E","year":2025,"venue":"Journal of Radiology Reporting","doi":"10.5555/jrr.2025.0011","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We analysed time stamps for 9,800 body CT reports before and after the introduction of structured templates. Median active reporting time increased by 1.4 minutes in the first month and returned to the pre-template level by the fourth month. Oncology staging reports remained about one minute longer throughout. Radiologists who had helped design the template returned to baseline faster. Time stamps do not capture interruptions, so active reporting time may be overestimated. Turnaround from scan to sign-off, which also depends on worklist order, changed less than active reporting time."}]}
